scenes.text: It's August 1912, in Chicago, in a hall full of Black business leaders.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: For two days, you've asked to speak. For two days, the answer is no.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: The man running this meeting is Booker T. Washington, one of the most powerful Black men in America.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: He thinks hair products are not serious business.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: So you stand up anyway, without being called.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: Surely, you tell him, you are not going to shut the door in my face.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

quote.text: Surely you are not going to shut the door in my face.

scenes.text: Twenty-five years ago, you were washing other people's clothes for about a dollar and a half a day.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: Seven years from now, you'll die in a mansion on the Hudson River.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: By the end, you'll know the one money rule that got you there,
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: and whether it still works today.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But to get here, we have to go back.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: It's December 23rd, 1867, and you're born in a cabin on a cotton plantation.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: Your name is Sarah Breedlove.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: Your parents, Owen and Minerva, were enslaved on this same plantation.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: The Civil War ended two years ago. You're the first child in your family born free.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: Keep count of three things: the money, the women working with you, and the doors closed in your face.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: Freedom doesn't pay much yet.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your family still picks cotton, now as sharecroppers: farmers who pay their rent with part of the crop.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: At the end of the season, the landowner's books somehow always say you owe him.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your mother dies when you're about five. Your father, a year or two later.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: By seven, you're an orphan.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: Your big sister, Louvenia, takes you in.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: sharecropper's log cabin in Delta, Louisiana, 1867: one room, a fireplace with an iron pot, a straw mattress on the floor, cotton fields through the open door, Mississippi River haze

scenes.text: In 1878, the two of you cross the river to Vicksburg, Mississippi.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: You're ten years old, and you work as a maid, scrubbing other people's floors.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: You get about three months of school in your whole life, at Sunday school.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: Louvenia's husband, Jesse Powell, is cruel to you, and the house is not safe.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: You see one way out.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: At fourteen, you marry a man named Moses McWilliams.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: Later you'll explain it simply: I married at the age of fourteen in order to get a home of my own.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

quote.text: I married at the age of fourteen in order to get a home of my own.

scenes.text: In 1885, you have a daughter. You name her Lelia.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: Remember that name. One day it'll be carved over the door of a mansion.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: The convention that won't let you speak is twenty-seven years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: Two years later, Moses dies. Nobody knows exactly how.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: You're nineteen, a widow, with a two-year-old and no money.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small wooden house kitchen in Vicksburg, Mississippi, 1880: wood stove, washboard and bucket, a steep hillside street and river boats through the window

scenes.text: Your four older brothers have moved to St. Louis, where they work as barbers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Barbers. Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So you take Lelia north on a riverboat, to a city of half a million people.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You find work as a washerwoman.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: You boil other families' laundry in a tub, scrub it on a board, and iron it by hand.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: For all that, you earn about a dollar and a half a day.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: Remember that number.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: You save enough to send Lelia to school. She'll get the education you never did.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: On Sundays, you go to St. Paul African Methodist Episcopal Church.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The church women there are teachers and club women. They wear neat dresses and neat hair.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You watch them, and you start to picture a different life.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1894, you marry again, a man named John Davis.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He drinks, and he's not faithful. By around 1903, it's over.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And then, in your thirties, something frightening starts to happen.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your hair is falling out.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's common among Black women of your time, and it's not mysterious.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Most homes have no indoor plumbing, so you wash your hair rarely, with harsh lye soap.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Add poor food, stress, and scalp infections, and the hair simply stops growing.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You ask your brothers the barbers for help. They know a lot about scalps.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You try every home remedy and store tonic you can find. Nothing works.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then, around 1903, you try a product made by a young St. Louis woman named Annie Turnbo.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Her Great Wonderful Hair Grower actually helps. Your hair starts coming back.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And Annie doesn't sell in stores. She sells through agents.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Here's the idea that will make you rich.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Imagine you bake the best bread in town, but you have only two hands.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You can bake maybe a hundred loaves a day. That's your ceiling.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Now teach a hundred neighbors your recipe, and sell each of them the flour.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: They bake and sell in their own streets, and keep the profit from every loaf they sell.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You earn a little on every bag of flour, a hundred times over.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's selling through agents: people who sell your product and keep a share for themselves.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: AGENT = SELLS FOR YOU, KEEPS A SHARE

scenes.text: You don't grow by working harder. You grow by making other people money.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You become one of Annie's agents, selling her grower door to door in St. Louis.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You're a good saleswoman. You know exactly what it feels like to lose your hair.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1904, the World's Fair comes to St. Louis.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: There you see Margaret Murray Washington, Booker T. Washington's wife, speak to a crowd of Black club women.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She's polished, educated, confident. You wonder if a washerwoman could ever stand on a stage like that.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The convention that won't let you speak is eight years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In July 1905, at thirty-seven, you take a train to Denver, Colorado.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You'll later say you arrived with about a dollar and fifty cents.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Denver has a lot of sun, very dry air, and almost no hair products for Black women.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You rent an attic room, and you sell Annie's grower as her Denver agent.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Denver attic room, 1905: sloping ceiling, a single iron bed, a wash basin, tins and jars on a shelf, the Rocky Mountains through a small window, bright dry light

scenes.text: To pay the rent, you also cook for a pharmacist named Edmund Scholtz.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Denver attic room, 1905: sloping ceiling, a single iron bed, a wash basin, tins and jars on a shelf, the Rocky Mountains through a small window, bright dry light

scenes.text: A pharmacist. Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Denver attic room, 1905: sloping ceiling, a single iron bed, a wash basin, tins and jars on a shelf, the Rocky Mountains through a small window, bright dry light

scenes.text: Then you have a dream.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Denver attic room, 1905: sloping ceiling, a single iron bed, a wash basin, tins and jars on a shelf, the Rocky Mountains through a small window, bright dry light

scenes.text: You'll say a big black man appeared to you and told you what to mix up for your hair.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Denver attic room, 1905: sloping ceiling, a single iron bed, a wash basin, tins and jars on a shelf, the Rocky Mountains through a small window, bright dry light

quote.text: A big black man appeared to me and told me what to mix up for my hair.

scenes.text: Some of the ingredients came from Africa, you'll say, and you sent away for them.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Denver attic room, 1905: sloping ceiling, a single iron bed, a wash basin, tins and jars on a shelf, the Rocky Mountains through a small window, bright dry light

scenes.text: Historians think the real recipe is more ordinary: petroleum jelly, sulfur, and a strong scent.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: Sulfur is an old treatment for scalp infections. The pharmacist you cook for may well have helped.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: Whatever the source, you mix it in your kitchen, pack it in tins, and test it on yourself.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: You call it Madam Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: Wait. Walker?
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: In January 1906, you marry Charles Joseph Walker, a newspaper advertising salesman.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He knows how to write ads, and he knows how to get them printed cheaply.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You take his name and add a French-sounding title. From now on, you're Madam C. J. Walker.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In the beauty trade, Madam sounds expensive. Which is the point.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Annie Turnbo is not pleased that her Denver agent now sells her own grower.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Her ads start warning customers to beware of imitators.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The two of you will be rivals for the rest of your life.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your ads show a before photo of you, short-haired, and an after photo with long hair.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The before photo is the washerwoman. The after photo is the brand.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: For eighteen months, you and C. J. travel the South, selling door to door.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You demonstrate in churches and lodges: you wash a woman's hair, treat her scalp, and press it smooth.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then you sell her the tin, for about fifty cents.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Soon you're making about ten dollars a day. Seven times what the washtub paid.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: C. J. thinks ten dollars a day is plenty. You'll later say he thought you were aiming too high.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: You don't want ten dollars a day. You want an empire.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: In 1908, you open a school in Pittsburgh, and call it Lelia College.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: Your daughter runs it. Lelia's all grown up.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: Here, women learn the Walker System: shampoo, grower, a brisk scalp massage, then a hot comb.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: They graduate as hair culturists: trained beauty workers who use only your products.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: Many of them used to be maids, cooks, and washerwomen. Like you.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: They pay for the course, buy your products at a discount, and sell them at full price.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: A Walker agent can earn several dollars a day. Some say up to fifteen.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: Remember the washtub? A dollar and a half a day.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: For a Black woman in 1908, there are very few jobs that pay like this, and no boss looking over her shoulder.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: Myth time. The internet says you invented the hot comb.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You didn't. Metal heated combs were already sold in Paris and in American catalogs.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your real invention isn't a tool. It's a business, built out of thousands of other women.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1910, you move the company to Indianapolis, a railroad hub in the middle of the country.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

scenes.text: Trains leave from here in every direction. So do your tins.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

scenes.text: You build a factory, a lab, a salon, and a training school.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

scenes.text: You hire a young lawyer named Freeman Ransom to run the business side.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1911, you incorporate. You are the sole shareholder.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: SOLE OWNER: MADAM C. J. WALKER

scenes.text: That same year, you give a thousand dollars to build a Black YMCA in Indianapolis.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's the kind of gift people expect from rich white men, not from a former washerwoman.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: C. J. wants a bigger say. He also, reportedly, wants other women.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: In 1912, you divorce him. You keep his name. It's on every tin.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: The convention that won't let you speak is now just months away.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small Denver kitchen turned workshop, 1906: a stove with simmering pots, rows of round tins with paper labels, mixing bowls, a hand-written recipe on the table

scenes.text: August 1912. Chicago. The National Negro Business League.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Booker T. Washington founded it to show the country what Black business can do.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Day after day, he calls on bankers, farmers, and undertakers. Not on you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: A friend asks him to give you a moment. Washington moves on.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So, on the last day, you stand up and take it.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: I am a woman who came from the cotton fields of the South, you tell the hall.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

quote.text: I am a woman who came from the cotton fields of the South.

scenes.text: I was promoted to the washtub, then to the cook kitchen.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: St. Louis back yard, 1890s: steaming wooden washtubs over a fire, washboards, lines of white sheets drying, brick tenements behind, smoky sky

scenes.text: And from there, you say, I promoted myself into the business of manufacturing hair goods.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

quote.text: I promoted myself into the business of manufacturing hair goods.

scenes.text: You tell them you've built your own factory on your own ground.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: The hall goes quiet. Washington doesn't reply. But he heard you.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

scenes.text: A year later, he invites you to speak from the stage.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The door that was shut in your face is now open. Remember that, too.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: By now, you have thousands of agents across the country.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

scenes.text: You sail to Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, Costa Rica, and Panama to recruit more.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You make sure you travel with tins. Every port is a market.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Meanwhile, Lelia moves to Harlem, in New York City, and opens a beauty salon there.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Years later, she'll change her name to A'Lelia. It sounds grander.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1916, you join her in Harlem, in a pair of townhouses on 136th Street.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Harlem is becoming the capital of Black America, and you want to be in the middle of it.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1917, you gather your agents in Philadelphia for a national convention.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's one of the first national meetings of American businesswomen, of any color.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You give prizes to the agents who sold the most.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And prizes to the agents who gave the most to charity.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: There is no royal flower-strewn path to success, you tell people.
scenes.speaker: narrator

quote.text: There is no royal flower-strewn path to success.

scenes.text: You also tell your agents: use your money and your voice.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That summer, white mobs in East St. Louis kill dozens of Black residents.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You join a delegation to the White House to ask President Wilson to act.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: outside the White House, Washington, 1917: iron fence and gate, the white columned portico across the lawn, a guard, summer trees

scenes.text: The President is too busy to see you. His secretary takes your petition instead.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: outside the White House, Washington, 1917: iron fence and gate, the white columned portico across the lawn, a guard, summer trees

scenes.text: Another door shut. This one, money can't open.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: outside the White House, Washington, 1917: iron fence and gate, the white columned portico across the lawn, a guard, summer trees

scenes.text: In 1918, you finish building a mansion in Irvington, on the Hudson River.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: Your neighbors are some of the richest white families in New York.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: They assume a Black woman this rich must be somebody's housekeeper.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: The architect is Vertner Tandy, the first licensed Black architect in New York State.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: You want the house to prove what a Black woman can build.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: The opera singer Enrico Caruso visits, and suggests a name.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: Lelia, Walker, Robinson: your daughter's married name at the time. Villa Lewaro.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: The little girl born in 1885 now has her name over the door.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: But your doctors have been warning you for years about your blood pressure.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You keep traveling anyway, and speaking, and selling.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In spring 1919, you pledge five thousand dollars to the NAACP's fight against lynching.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It's the biggest single gift that fund has ever received.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Weeks later, on May 25th, 1919, you die at Villa Lewaro of kidney failure.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: You're fifty-one years old.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York, 1918: grand Italianate mansion with columns, a terrace with stone balustrade, gardens, the Hudson River and Palisades beyond

scenes.text: Your will leaves a third of your estate to A'Lelia, and two-thirds of future profits to charity.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: A'Lelia will turn your Harlem home into a famous salon for writers and artists.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So, how did a washerwoman end up with a mansion on the Hudson?
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Myth number two: you're often called America's first self-made female millionaire.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your estate was valued at about six hundred thousand dollars. Close, but not a million.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's roughly eleven million dollars today. Not bad for someone with three months of school.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And it was never the money that mattered most.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Tens of thousands of women learned a trade under your name, and kept their own earnings.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

scenes.text: Many of them would never wash another stranger's sheets.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

scenes.text: You once summed it up: I got my start by giving myself a start.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, 1911: brick workroom, women in white aprons filling and labeling round tins at long tables, crates stamped WALKER, tall factory windows

quote.text: I got my start by giving myself a start.

scenes.text: Here's the money rule.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: MONEY RULE: GROW BY MAKING OTHERS EARN

scenes.text: The rule: your income can only grow as far as the people you help earn.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Picture a hairdresser who cuts ten heads a day at forty dollars each. Four hundred a day, maximum.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Now she rents five chairs to other stylists for two hundred a week each.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That's another thousand a week, and five people building their own businesses.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But here's where the rule goes wrong.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Many modern direct-selling schemes copy your model, and most of their sellers earn little or lose money.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The test is simple: do people earn from real customers, or only from recruiting more people?
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your agents had real customers, who came back every month because the hair grew back.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: You didn't get rich off women. You got rich with them.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Lelia College beauty school in Pittsburgh, 1908: bright parlor classroom, rows of chairs with students, washbasins, combs and tins on a counter, a chalkboard, lace curtains

scenes.text: Some doors open when you knock. The rest, you build.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: Chicago meeting hall, 1912: raised wooden stage with a long table and a podium, rows of wooden chairs, bunting with 'National Negro Business League' banner, tall windows, afternoon light

meta.thumbnail: You, in a pearl-collared dress, standing on a hall stage holding a round tin of hair grower, a washtub behind you; text: 'FROM $1.50'
meta.description:
Born free on a Louisiana plantation, orphaned at seven, washing clothes for $1.50 a day.
Then you build an army of saleswomen and a mansion on the Hudson.

A comedic dramatization of documented history.

Sources:
A'Lelia Bundles, On Her Own Ground: The Life and Times of Madam C. J. Walker (2001)
Madam C. J. Walker Papers, Indiana Historical Society
National Park Service and Smithsonian NMAAHC articles on Madam C. J. Walker
factCheck: Born Sarah Breedlove, 23 Dec 1867, Delta, Madison Parish, Louisiana, on the Burney plantation; parents Owen and Minerva had been enslaved; first child born free (Bundles; Indiana Historical Society)
Mother died ~1872, father ~1875 (dates vary by source; 'about' used)
Moved to Vicksburg with sister Louvenia ~1878; brother-in-law Jesse Powell's cruelty (Walker's own account)
Said she had only about three months of formal schooling, in Sunday school (Walker's account via Bundles)
Married Moses McWilliams 1882 at 14; daughter Lelia born 6 June 1885; Moses died ~1887, cause unknown
Moved to St. Louis ~1888 where her brothers were barbers; laundress earning about $1.50 a day (Bundles)
St. Paul AME Church, St. Louis; married John Davis 1894, separated by ~1903
Hair loss from scalp disorders, harsh soaps, infrequent washing (Bundles; Smithsonian)
Became Annie Turnbo (later Malone) agent ~1903-1904; Turnbo's products sold via agents
1904 St. Louis World's Fair; heard Margaret Murray Washington at the National Association of Colored Women meeting (Bundles)
Moved to Denver July 1905 with about $1.50 by her own later account; cooked for pharmacist Edmund L. Scholtz
Dream story from Walker's own 1917-18 interviews; formula likely petrolatum, sulfur and scent (Bundles; analyses of the product)
Married Charles Joseph Walker Jan 1906; became Madam C. J. Walker
Turnbo ads warned against imitators; long rivalry
Traveled ~18 months 1906-1908; C. J. thought $10/day was enough (Walker's account); tins ~50 cents
Lelia College, Pittsburgh, 1908; 'hair culturists'; agents earned about $5-$15 a day by Walker's advertising claims
Hot comb not invented by Walker: heated metal combs sold in France and US catalogs before 1900
Moved to Indianapolis 1910; factory, lab, school; Freeman B. Ransom attorney; incorporated 1911 with Walker as sole shareholder
$1,000 pledge to Indianapolis Black YMCA, 1911
Divorced C. J. Walker ~1912
National Negro Business League, Chicago, Aug 1912: Washington ignored her; she spoke unbidden on the last day; invited to speak in 1913
Caribbean/Central America trip 1913-14 (Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, Costa Rica, Panama)
A'Lelia opened Harlem salon 1913; Walker moved to 108-110 W. 136th St. 1916
Philadelphia convention of the Madam C. J. Walker Hair Culturists Union of America, Aug 1917, ~200 agents; prizes for sales and philanthropy
East St. Louis massacre July 1917; delegation to White House Aug 1917 not received by Wilson
Villa Lewaro, Irvington NY, 34 rooms, completed 1918; architect Vertner Tandy, first licensed Black architect in NY; name suggested by Enrico Caruso from Lelia Walker Robinson
$5,000 pledge to NAACP anti-lynching fund, May 1919, its largest single gift at the time
Died 25 May 1919 at Villa Lewaro, age 51, kidney failure from hypertension
Will: company to A'Lelia; one-third of net profits to charity
Estate ~ $600,000 (Bundles); 'first self-made female millionaire' is a popular claim not supported by the estate value; ~$11M today using CPI x ~18.5 (1919-2026)
Modern example numbers are illustrative; FTC research: most direct-selling/MLM participants earn little or lose money
sources: A'Lelia Bundles, On Her Own Ground (Scribner, 2001), quotes from the 1912 NNBL speech: 'Surely you are not going to shut the door in my face', 'I am a woman who came from the cotton fields of the South', 'I promoted myself into the business of manufacturing hair goods'
Proceedings of the National Negro Business League, 1912 (Walker's speech)
'I married at the age of fourteen in order to get a home of my own' and dream account: Walker interviews, Kansas City Star 1917 / New York Times Magazine 1917, via Bundles
'There is no royal flower-strewn path to success' and 'I got my start by giving myself a start': Walker, quoted in Bundles and madamcjwalker.com
Indiana Historical Society, Madam C. J. Walker Papers: https://indianahistory.org
FTC, Business Guidance Concerning Multi-Level Marketing: https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/business-guidance-concerning-multi-level-marketing
